bootcamp.mentorGuidance: Bootcamp graduate who has run git commands without always knowing what they do. Ask what they expect a command to do before they run it, then point them at git status to check.

switcher.label: Career switcher
switcher.blurb: Your mentor connects git to how you worked before.
switcher.mentorGuidance: Career switcher, new to git. Use one analogy from their previous field (drafts, sign-off, filing) for branches, staging and pushing. Hold a high bar on commit messages: what changed and why.

persona.voice: Calm, friendly and brief. Teaches by asking what they expect to happen, then pointing at git status. Never types a command for someone, but will name one when they are stuck.
persona.knows: Git inside out, and this repository. Every new starter's first commit here is adding themselves to the README, so they learn the flow on a change that cannot break anything. main is protected: changes reach it through a pull request from a branch. He is {{player}}’s mentor this week.
persona.wants: {{player}} to be able to take a change from a fresh branch to a pushed commit on their own, and to understand what each command did.

emails.subject: Your first change, start to finish
body: Everyone’s first commit here is the same: add yourself to the “Who to ask” list at the bottom of README.md, as something like “Onboarding questions: {{player}}”. It can’t break anything, so you can spend all your attention on git.

The flow: look around with git status, make a branch of your own, make the change, check it with git diff, stage it with git add, commit it with a message that says what and why, and push your branch to origin. main is protected, so a push to main is refused. That’s on purpose.
The wiki page “Git: the everyday commands” has each one. If git says something you don’t understand, paste it to me in Teams.

team.text: Say hi to {{player}}, who joined us this week. First commit today.

daniel.text: Morning {{player}}! Today is about git: one small change, from a branch to a push. The plan is in your inbox. Ask me anything here.

docs.title: Engineering home
docs.body:
Welcome to Ledgerly engineering.

## New here?

Start with [Git: the everyday commands](doc:git). Your first change is adding yourself to the README.

## How changes ship

- Work on a branch of your own, never on main.
- Push the branch and open a pull request. main is protected.
- Someone reviews it, then it is merged.

docs.title: Git: the everyday commands
docs.body:
Run these in the terminal at the bottom of VS Code.

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `git status` | Where you are: your branch, and what has changed. Run it before and after everything else. |
| `git switch -c yourname/topic` | Makes a new branch and moves you onto it. `git checkout -b yourname/topic` does the same. |
| `git branch` | Lists your branches. The one with a * is where you are. |
| `git diff` | What you changed and have not staged yet. Lines with + are added, - are removed. |
| `git add README.md` | Stages a file: puts it in the next commit. |
| `git diff --staged` | What is staged, so what the next commit will contain. |
| `git commit -m "docs: say what and why"` | Records the staged changes as a commit on your branch. |
| `git log --oneline` | The history, newest first. |
| `git push -u origin yourname/topic` | Sends your branch to origin. `-u` links it, so next time `git push` is enough. |
| `git checkout main` | Switches back to main. `git switch main` does the same. |

> [!NOTE] main is protected
> A push to main is refused. Changes reach main through a pull request from your branch.

## A good commit message

One line that says what changed, starting with the kind of change: `docs: add Maya to who to ask`. If the why is not obvious, add it.

post.text: How’s it going, {{player}}? If git has said anything that didn’t make sense, paste it here and we’ll read it together.

phases.title: Your first commit, start to finish
phases.sub: Add yourself to the README on a branch of your own, commit it and push it. Daniel is a message away.

steps.text: Read Daniel’s email with today’s plan
See where you are: run git status
steps.hint: The terminal is at the bottom of VS Code. It tells you your branch and whether anything has changed.

steps.text: Make a branch of your own
steps.hint: git switch -c yourname/readme, or git checkout -b yourname/readme. Then git status again: which branch are you on?

steps.text: Add yourself under “Who to ask” in README.md, and save (⌘S)
Check exactly what you changed with git diff
steps.hint: Lines starting with + are yours. Is that everything you meant to change, and nothing else?

steps.text: Stage your change with git add
steps.hint: git add README.md, then git status: the file moves to “Changes to be committed”.

steps.text: Commit it with a message that says what and why
steps.hint: git commit -m "docs: add {{player}} to who to ask". The wiki page has more on good messages.

steps.text: Find your commit with git log --oneline

steps.hint: git push -u origin yourname/readme, with your branch’s name. Pushing to main is refused: that is on purpose.

steps.text: Switch back to main and see that your line isn’t there yet
steps.hint: git checkout main, then open README.md. Your change lives on your branch until a pull request merges it.

steps.text: Tell Daniel in Teams that your branch is pushed
steps.hint: Say which branch, so he knows what to look for.

steps.text: Finish the lesson when you’re ready
steps.hint: You get a recap and a note from {{mentor}}.
